text: Framework knitters in Nottinghamshire began breaking the machines that undercut their trade. The Luddite movement spread across northern England until 1816.
Cavalry charged a peaceful crowd of around 60,000 demanding parliamentary reform at St Peter’s Field, Manchester. The Peterloo Massacre killed at least 15 people.
Six farm labourers from Tolpuddle, Dorset, were sentenced to transportation to Australia for swearing an oath to a union. Public outcry won their pardon in 1836.
Strikes spread through Britain’s industrial north as workers pulled the plugs from factory boilers. The Plug Plot strikes are often called the first general strike.
The Manifesto of the Communist Party was published in London, written by Marx and Engels for the Communist League.
Volume one of Marx’s Capital was published in Hamburg in an edition of 1,000 copies. It took four years to sell out.
The Paris Commune took control of the city and governed for 72 days before its suppression in the Bloody Week of May.
A bomb at a Chicago rally for the eight-hour day led to the Haymarket trial. The executions of four anarchists made May 1 an international workers’ day.
Women and girls at the Bryant & May match factory in London walked out over fines, wages and phosphorus poisoning, and won.
London dockers struck for sixpence an hour, the “dockers’ tanner.” Their five-week victory opened the era of mass unskilled unionism in Britain.
The Pullman strike shut down rail traffic across the western US until federal troops broke it. Eugene Debs went to jail and came out a socialist.
Sheriff’s deputies fired on unarmed striking miners near Lattimer, Pennsylvania, killing 19. Most of the dead were Polish, Slovak and Lithuanian immigrants.
The Industrial Workers of the World was founded in Chicago, aiming to organize all workers regardless of skill, race or sex into “one big union.”
The Uprising of the 20,000 began when garment workers in New York, most of them young immigrant women, voted for a general strike of the shirtwaist trade.
At a socialist women’s conference in Copenhagen, Clara Zetkin and others proposed an annual International Women’s Day.
Fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York killed 146 garment workers, many trapped behind locked doors. It reshaped labor safety law.
Textile workers in Lawrence, Massachusetts, speaking dozens of languages, struck for two months over a pay cut and won. It is remembered as the Bread and Roses strike.
Rosa Luxemburg published The Accumulation of Capital, arguing that capitalism depends on expanding into non-capitalist regions.
The Dublin Lockout began when employers locked out members of Jim Larkin’s Irish Transport and General Workers’ Union. It lasted into 1914.
Colorado National Guard troops attacked a tent colony of striking coal miners at Ludlow. Two women and eleven children died in a pit beneath a burning tent.
Women textile workers in Petrograd struck on International Women’s Day. Within days the strike had become the February Revolution.
About 65,000 workers in Seattle stopped work in a five-day general strike, and strike committees ran milk delivery and food kitchens across the city.
Around 10,000 armed coal miners fought company guards and police at Blair Mountain, West Virginia, the largest armed uprising in the US since the Civil War.
The British General Strike began in support of locked-out coal miners. The TUC called it off after nine days.
State police opened fire on striking coal miners at the Columbine Mine in Serene, Colorado, killing six. The strike was led by the IWW.
Black Tuesday. Over the next three years US industrial production fell by nearly half, and by 1933 roughly a quarter of the workforce was unemployed.
General strikes in San Francisco, Minneapolis and Toledo turned the tide of US labor. Each was led in part by radicals: communists, Trotskyists and Musteites.
The National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act) guaranteed most US private-sector workers the right to organize and bargain collectively.
After 44 days of autoworkers occupying its Flint plants, General Motors recognized the United Auto Workers.
Chicago police shot at strikers and supporters picnicking outside Republic Steel, killing ten. It became known as the Memorial Day Massacre.
The Fair Labor Standards Act set the first US federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour and moved toward a 40-hour week.
Karl Polanyi published The Great Transformation, arguing that a self-regulating market was a utopia that society would always resist.
Congress passed the Taft–Hartley Act over Truman’s veto, banning secondary boycotts and allowing states to pass right-to-work laws.
Five former students of a local priest, José María Arizmendiarrieta, started a paraffin-stove workshop in Mondragón. It grew into one of the world’s largest federations of worker cooperatives.
E. P. Thompson published The Making of the English Working Class, arguing that class is something that happens in human relationships rather than a fixed structure.
Filipino farmworkers in the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee walked out of Delano grape fields. Chavez and Huerta’s farmworkers’ association joined them a week later.
Black sanitation workers in Memphis struck after two colleagues were crushed in a garbage truck. Their signs read “I AM A MAN.”
About 200,000 US postal workers staged a wildcat strike, the largest in the agency’s history. It won them collective bargaining rights.
Nixon suspended the dollar’s convertibility into gold, ending the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates.
Harry Braverman published Labor and Monopoly Capital, a study of how management deskills work, which launched the labor process debate.
Strikers at the Gdańsk shipyard signed an agreement with the Polish government that led to the founding of Solidarność, an independent trade union.
Reagan fired more than 11,000 striking air traffic controllers in PATCO, a signal to employers that permanent replacement of strikers was acceptable.
The Volcker shock pushed the US federal funds rate to around 20%, breaking inflation and accelerating the collapse of industrial employment.
The UK miners’ strike began over pit closures and lasted almost a year, one of the longest major strikes in British history.
US union membership peaked at roughly a third of wage and salary workers in the mid-1950s. Today it is about one in ten.
